findings.speaker: any (comp)
findings.text: 絵も、やっと帰ってきたね。
findings.en: The picture's finally come home.
findings.why: In the source this is `?(comp) comp[smile]:` with no companion branch, so Ren can say it. Ren speaks です/ます to the player throughout the game, post-game included (atlas.*: 〜ですよね, 参りましょう), so a bare 〜たね from Ren would sound out of character. It fits Nao, Suzu, and Mio in her plain stretches.
findings.direction: Branch it by companion, or at least give Ren a polite variant (e.g. Ren: 「絵も、やっと帰ってこられましたね。」). Nao could take 〜な.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion after the whole journey, post-game: close)
findings.text: 店の看板に「定休日」を書き足しました。……初めて書いた字です。
findings.en: I added "Regular day off" to the shop sign. …First time I've ever written those words.
findings.why: This banter is gated `if: 'post'`. Every other post-game Mio line to the player is soft plain (atlas.home 「お茶、淹れるね」, end.mio.b 「……水曜以外ならね」, end.mio.core), so here she suddenly sounds as distant as she did on day one.
findings.direction: Use her post-game soft plain register, e.g. 「…書き足したの。……初めて書いた字。」

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion; plays on any return to Reedwake, mid-journey or post-game)
findings.text: 旅の荷物、三回確かめました。……薬が一本多いんです。誰かが入れた？……私ですね。心配で。
findings.en: I checked our packs three times. …There's one bottle too many. Did someone put it in? …It was me. I was worried.
findings.why: The banter entry has no condition, so it plays whenever Mio is the companion on an rw.* map. That only happens after departure, when she has already gone plain with the player (sg.* banter, atlas.*), but the line is fully です/ます. The content (checking packs) also sounds like the start of a journey.
findings.direction: Either gate it to early in the journey, or give it her companion plain register, e.g. 「…三回確かめたの。……薬が一本多い。誰かが入れた？……私だね。」

findings.speaker: mio
findings.text: 雨が降ったら濡れてしまいます。持っていきましょう。
findings.en: If it rains, it'll get soaked. Let's keep it with us.
findings.why: Every Mio line to the player in the case files is です/ます: cs.parcel_oldsite#50446db2e6, cs.talk_parcel#29389180ef and #bfca5017e2, cs.talk_view#b0b6b8e84e and #b9b8d76e72. On the same Saltglass beach and quay, every sg.* line from her to the player is plain (sg.arrive 「…分かってるよ」, sg.da_reading_first 「生姜の飴、あげる」), so she flips register between a case line and a story line in the same town. Her lines in front of NPCs (cs.view_window to Genzō, cs.shell_shiori) are fine polite.
findings.direction: Case talk lines can play in any chapter, so either write them in a register that holds across her arc or branch them by chapter. The Saltglass-located ones should match sg.* plain, e.g. 「雨が降ったら濡れちゃう。持っていこう。」

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: 先生なら、どうしたでしょう。教えは全部覚えているのに、顔が……いえ、関係ない話です。
findings.en: What would my teacher have done? I remember every lesson, and yet the face… No. That's beside the point.
findings.why: Ren calls their missing teacher 先生 only in Reedwake (7 times) and 師匠 in every other region (70+, including sg.b_ren_archive#8839e61f09 and sg.ch2_end#114283d6ab in this part). The English also switches from 'teacher' to 'master'. The person is central to the plot, and 先生 and 師匠 imply different relationships, so a listener will notice. The post-game rw.b_ren2 still says 先生 while post-game atlas.camp says 師匠. The other 先生 lines are rw.b_ren2#a34ab4e1fa, rw.hall_ren#c6cdf47029, rw.mr_ren#962f62ad76, rw.mr_lantern#7686da0cd8 (VA2), rw.ren_lanterns_done#9d1ca6e587 and rw.ren_after#f86d1cfa6c.
findings.direction: Pick one term for Ren's teacher before recording and use it everywhere. 師匠 fits a keeper's apprenticeship and is the majority form. Align the English to match.

findings.speaker: hana
findings.text: いらっしゃい！……ごめんなさい、今朝の混む時間で。コウジが戻ったって聞いて、みんな見に来るのよ。手伝ってくれる？
findings.en: Welcome! …Sorry, it's the morning rush. Everyone heard Kōji's back and came to look. Would you help?
findings.why: The source has the reading {今|いま}{朝|あさ} ('now, it's the morning rush'), but the plain script shows 今朝, which a voice actor will read けさ. 「けさの混む時間で」 is also odd Japanese.
findings.direction: Separate the words so they cannot fuse into 今朝, e.g. 「ごめんなさい、今、朝の混む時間で。」 or 「ちょうど朝の混む時間なの。」

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: Sae, then pc (acquaintance of a day; Mio is not yet a companion)
findings.text: よく言えました。……私はここでサエさんといる。気をつけてね。
findings.en: Well said. …I'll stay here with Sae. Be careful.
findings.why: The second half is spoken to the player (Sae is in the third person, サエさん). Mio is です/ます to the player in every surrounding ch1 scene, including the next one (rw.mr_mio2: 「次はあなたの番ですよ。ちゃんと帰ってきてください」). Plain 〜といる。気をつけてね reads as leftover from her gentle register with Sae. The bare 「サエさんといる」 is also abrupt.
findings.direction: Make the turn to the player polite, e.g. 「私はここでサエさんといます。気をつけてくださいね。」, or stage it so it is clearly still said to Sae.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: ……ありがとう。灯りが一つともると、道が一つ思い出す。先生の口癖です。
findings.en: …Thank you. Light one lantern and the road remembers one thing. My teacher used to say that.
findings.why: 思い出す has no object. The floating 一つ after 道が reads as counting roads ('one road remembers…'), not as 'the road remembers one thing'. Read aloud, the saying sounds broken rather than poetic.
findings.direction: If the meaning is 'the road remembers one thing', make the object explicit, e.g. 「灯りが一つともると、道が名前を一つ思い出す」. If the ambiguity is intended, keep it and add a note. The 先生 here is covered by the 先生/師匠 finding.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: ……棚に上げられたのかもしれません。
findings.en: …Perhaps it's been shelved.
findings.why: This is the learner's first 棚に上げる, used as a literal-plus-pun 'put on the archive's shelf'. The real idiom means 'conveniently ignore (one's own faults)', and English 'shelved' suggests 'postponed', so learners will take away the wrong meaning. The motif continues in this part (Clerk sg.da_boss#eb493c4504 「返送し、棚に上げ」, sg.da_boss_after#0641a37bf3, PC sg.ch2_end#5fd13874f4) and pays off later when Kasane uses the true idiom (sa.toya_read).
findings.direction: No text change. Add a note at this first occurrence giving the idiom's real meaning and marking this use as Ren's literal pun.

findings.speaker: tsuru
findings.text: そこの旅の人。泥だらけだね。灯の道から来たのかい。
findings.en: You there, traveller. You're covered in mud. Did you come by the lantern road?
findings.why: This is the first sentence-final かい, Tsuru's signature (〜かい appears 10+ times in Reedwake). It is an older, friendly-gruff question marker, not a neutral model. The automated word-help report lists かい as mis-mapped to 回 (counter).
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note: のかい／かい is a familiar question ending used mostly by older speakers; learners should use 〜の？／〜ですか.

findings.speaker: tsuru
findings.text: でも、あんたの字は残った。手を貸しておくれ。宿と飯くらいは出すよ。
findings.en: But your writing held. Lend me a hand. I can at least give you a bed and meals.
findings.why: This is the first 〜ておくれ, an old-fashioned elder request form that recurs (rw.bridge_scene 「来ておくれ」, rw.tsuru_first 「聞いておくれ」). Learners have no way to tell that it is 〜てくれ softened and marked as elderly, not something to copy.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note: おくれ = くれ, old-fashioned, typical of older speakers.

findings.speaker: oto
findings.text: ついでに、あの灯守の若いのに言っておくれ。靴くらい持って来いって。見てるだけで足が冷たくなる。
findings.en: While you're at it, tell that young lantern keeper to bring me their boots. Just looking at them makes my feet cold.
findings.why: Oto is an adult, brisk tradesperson, yet here takes Tsuru's elderly markers (〜ておくれ, and 「見てくれるかい」 in #a4851d316b). That ages Oto up and blurs the elder voice that makes Tsuru distinctive. The same おくれ goes to middle-aged Kiyo (sg.dir_kiyo#666fe864f6 「持って帰ってきておくれ」) and Tamae (sg.b_suzu_debt#9ec439dc69 「一曲やっておくれ」). Those two are more defensible as hearty market-auntie speech but follow the same pattern.
findings.direction: Give Oto brisk adult forms (e.g. 「言っといてくれ」／「見てくれる？」). Decide whether おくれ belongs only to the elder generation (Tsuru) and use it sparingly elsewhere.

findings.speaker: bunta
findings.text: キクの婆さんが、春に貸したかんなを返さねえんだ。道具の名札も嵐で白くなっちまって、証拠もねえ。
findings.en: Old Kiku won't give back the plane I lent her in spring. And the storm wiped the name tags off my tools, so I've got no proof.
findings.why: The line is right for Bunta. It packs three rough forms into one line on the learner's first meeting with this register: ねえ for ない (twice) and ちまって for てしまって. 婆さん is also blunt.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a word-help or register note for 〜ねえ = 〜ない and 〜ちまう = 〜てしまう as rough casual masculine speech.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: nobody / the gulls (performative), with pc beside her
findings.text: さあさあ、お立ち会い！潮とガラスの町、潮硝子にご到着！
findings.en: Roll up, roll up! Now arriving: the town of tide and glass, Saltglass!
findings.why: お立ち会い is a traditional street-performer's call, and ご到着 is mock-honorific announcing. Both are right for Suzu, but a learner cannot tell they are a stage formula and not ordinary politeness. The same applies to 「旅のお方！」 in rw.suzu_first#9fa6f75f9e (VA1:SUZU02, VA2).
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note that this is a barker's or stage call, used jokingly.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 帳簿を合わせるための嘘は、一つでは終わらないの。……会いに行きましょう。
findings.en: A lie told to balance the books never stays just one lie. …Let's go and see him.
findings.kansai: 帳簿合わせるための嘘は、一つでは終わらへんねん。……会いに行こうか。
findings.why: The standard line ends in a firm ます-volitional (行きましょう), a deliberate step up from Suzu's usual plain. The Kansai line changes it to plain, tentative 行こうか, which shifts both politeness and resolve instead of only the dialect.
findings.direction: Make the two versions match. Either both plain and firm (standard 「会いに行こう」 / Kansai 「会いに行こ」), or both ます-form (Kansai e.g. 「会いに行きましょ」).

findings.speaker: pc
findings.text: この小包、あなた宛ではありませんか。
findings.en: Could this parcel be for you?
findings.why: Using あなた directly to a stranger tradesperson is English-shaped. Polite spoken Japanese avoids it, and the parcel is addressed to the workshop, not a name.
findings.direction: e.g. 「この小包、こちら宛ではありませんか。」

findings.speaker: mio
findings.text: 誰も触ってないのに、字が動いてる。葦ノ瀬と同じ……。
findings.en: No one's touched it and the writing moves. Just like in Reedwake…
findings.why: The narration has just said 「誰も触っていない。字だけが、勝手に動いている。」 Mio's line, and Nao's #bb752c9d2f, open with the same clause again almost word for word, so the companions narrate what the player is looking at.
findings.direction: Keep the reactions (Nao 「……気味が悪いな」, Mio 「葦ノ瀬と同じ……」) and cut or vary the restated clause.

findings.speaker: cs_hama
findings.text: 名前が書いてなくても、仕事を続けている人がいれば、宛名は生きているものだね。
findings.en: Even with no name on it — as long as someone's still doing the job, the address stays alive.
findings.why: A practical quay repair-keeper states the case's moral aloud. In this part, case-reward NPCs routinely end on a maxim (Tokuji cs.spool_tokuji#cfd69736e6 「水門も、町もな」, Shiori cs.shell_shiori#e0d5320235 「正しければそれでいいのです」). Together these drift toward the 'every character an oracle' effect the spec warns against.
findings.direction: Let Hama react concretely (the bell, the old master, how long the order took) and leave the moral implicit or to the companion's talk line.

findings.speaker: kiku
findings.text: まあ、私の杼。……ブンタさん、自分で来られないのね。照れ屋だこと。
findings.en: Oh, my shuttle. …Bunta couldn't bring it himself, I see. Such a shy man.
findings.why: 〜だこと is a marked, older-feminine exclamatory ending. It is right for Kiku but opaque to learners, who may read it as the nominaliser こと.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note that 〜（だ）こと is an exclamation ('how…!') in older, refined feminine speech.

findings.speaker: shiori
findings.addressee: pc (stranger, visitor at the tide-watch hut)
findings.text: 急がなくていいですよ。知らない言葉は、言葉の手助けで読み方と意味が分かります。
findings.en: There's no hurry. If a word is new, word help will give you its reading and meaning.
findings.why: The tide-keeper describes the game's word-help UI feature in-world (「言葉の手助け」 is not a thing in her world), so a UI tutorial leaks into character speech. Said aloud, it sounds like a help screen in her voice.
findings.direction: Keep only the in-character half (急がなくていいですよ / the table is always here) and move the word-help hint to UI or system text, not recorded dialogue.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc / Yasu (elderly acquaintance) at the moment he recalls Koharuno
findings.text: よかった……。ヤスさん、顔色が変わりました。
findings.en: Oh, good… Yasu's colour has come back.
findings.why: 顔色が変わる means a sudden change of expression, usually going pale from shock or anger, so after よかった it means the opposite of the intended 'his colour has come back'. A native listener would hear alarm, not relief. It reads like a literal rendering of the English.
findings.direction: Use an expression that means 'looks better', e.g. 顔色がよくなりました or 顔に血の気が戻りました.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (travelling companion, same relationship stage as in ch2)
findings.text: 空気が乾いていますね。柿を干すにはいいけど……喉を痛める人が多そう。
findings.en: The air's so dry. Good for drying persimmons, but… I'd guess a lot of sore throats.
findings.why: Mio speaks to the PC in です/ます in ch1 (cs.*), then in consistent soft plain through all of ch2 Saltglass (some 60 lines, e.g. sg.road_inland_closed 今、確かに北へ歩いたよね？, sg.b_mio_* bond talks), then goes back to です/ます from her first ch3 lines (here, co.arrive#3f4e28b1bc …みたいです, co.ashband#f512e1c650 灰の層です, co.ashband#c1ea4eb674 …一番です) and on into sb. Nothing in the story motivates going back to polite after a chapter of plain, and it reverses the intended softening. Lines in this part that already follow the polite pattern toward the PC: sg.lw_road_child#9d10a74e9f, lq.kayo_idle#c97d2947aa, lq.road_write#d5fef45118.
findings.direction: Robin to fix Mio's register toward the PC for each chapter or bond stage (e.g. soft polite with plain slips that become more frequent), then align the ch2 sg block or the ch3/ch4 lines with it before recording. Do not flatten her polite speech to strangers.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion, light banter after helping a lost child)
findings.text: 灯台が見えた時の顔、見ました？一番のお薬ですね。
findings.en: Did you see that face when the lighthouse came into view? Better than any medicine.
findings.why: Inside ch2 this is the only line where Mio uses です/ます toward the PC. Every other sg line to the PC is plain (sg.road_bench おいしいだろうね, sg.return_harbor 見て、…よかった), so in this light banter it sounds like a sudden step back. It comes from the living-world author pass, not the ch2 script.
findings.direction: Match whatever Robin decides for Mio's ch2 register (see co.arrive#c99094f2db); if ch2 stays plain, e.g. 見た？.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: Wataru (adult stranger met that day, has just confessed)
findings.text: 言ってくれて、ありがとう。……でも、優しくするのと、許すのは違う。港長さんにも、灯台にも、ちゃんと言わなきゃ。
findings.en: Thank you for telling us. …But being kind isn't the same as letting it go. You have to tell the harbourmaster, and the lighthouse, properly.
findings.why: Mio is polite to every other adult stranger in ch2 (Genzō, Ōmi, Tetsu). Here she lectures a man she met that day in plain speech, so the moral line ('kindness isn't forgiveness') sounds talked-down, which is the condescension she herself hates. The warm thanks could stay soft, but the instruction lands better in polite speech.
findings.direction: Keep the warmth and move the sentences that tell him what to do into soft polite, e.g. …許すのとは違います。…ちゃんと言わないと.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 二枚看板ってやつだね！……真面目に言うと、戦いであんたが狙われたら、客の目は私が引き受ける。二人で一組の芸だからね。
findings.en: A double bill! …Seriously, though: if something takes aim at you in a fight, I'll draw the audience's eye. We're a two-person act.
findings.why: Suzu's standard line uses あんた for the PC. Across the game her standard voice uses あなた for the PC (about 30 lines) and keeps あんた for the Kansai version. Here the Kansai pronoun has leaked into the standard text, which makes standard Suzu rougher, closer to Nao, at a tender moment.
findings.direction: Use あなた in the standard line and keep あんた in KANSAI.

findings.speaker: yasu
findings.text: ……だが、村の名前が出てこん。女房が死んでから、誰もあの名前を口にしなくなった。気がついたら、わしの頭からも消えとった。
findings.en: …But the name won't come. After my wife died, nobody said it anymore. Before I knew it, it had gone out of my head too.
findings.why: Only in the lq quest does Yasu switch to generic stage-old-man forms: わし ×4 (also lq.road_yasu1#f623fdcb51, lq.road_write#f1d930c6d2, #281644c844, lq.road_yasu2#e9e069f801) and the western/role-language 〜とった. In his other scenes he says 俺 (dv.yasu#e4b24ae510) and speaks plain standard with 〜ん. The pronoun change and the dialect form come from his age, not his established voice.
findings.direction: Pick one first-person pronoun for Yasu across the game and drop 〜とった unless he is meant to have a regional voice everywhere, e.g. 消えていた / 消えちまった.

findings.speaker: pc
findings.addressee: Chigusa (older woman, met minutes ago; PC has just used her name)
findings.text: 最後まで、あなたを待っていたそうです。「約束したんだから、どこかで生きてる」って。
findings.en: She waited for you to the end. "They promised — so they're alive somewhere," she used to say.
findings.why: Addressing an older person whose name you know as あなた, in polite speech, sounds distant and English-shaped; Japanese would use the name or drop the object. Since the PC's lines model speech for learners, this matters more than usual.
findings.direction: Use the name or drop the object, e.g. 最後まで、チグサさんを待っていたそうです.

findings.speaker: pc
findings.addressee: Kayo (older acquaintance, addressed as カヨさん in the line before)
findings.text: 柿の木に、あなたの背の線が残っていました。
findings.en: Your height marks are still on the persimmon tree.
findings.why: This is a player choice, so a model sentence. The PC has just called her カヨさん, and switching to あなた for an older acquaintance is the textbook learner mistake the game should not model.
findings.direction: e.g. 柿の木に、カヨさんの背の線が残っていました.

findings.speaker: pc
findings.addressee: a small lost child, near tears
findings.text: 今は急いでいる。ごめんね。
findings.en: We're in a hurry just now. Sorry.
findings.why: A bare dictionary-form 急いでいる。 as a full sentence reads like narration and sounds cold to a child. It also clashes with the soft ごめんね that follows. Spoken refusals give a reason with ん/て.
findings.direction: Make it a spoken excuse, e.g. 今、ちょっと急いでるんだ。ごめんね.

findings.speaker: shiori
findings.text: いらっしゃいませ。今日の潮を聞きにいらっしゃったのですか。
findings.en: Welcome. Have you come to ask about today's tide?
findings.why: Two いらっしゃ forms back to back sound clumsy aloud, and the written-style のですか makes the greeting stiffer than her precise-polite voice needs. いらっしゃいませ is also a shop greeting for what is a public hut (she uses it in sg.shiori_early too).
findings.direction: Keep her polite precision but avoid the repetition, e.g. 潮のことでいらしたんですか / 今日の潮のお尋ねですか.

findings.speaker: shiori
findings.text: 霧はまだ座っています。風のことは、ゲンゾウさんに。
findings.en: The fog is still sitting there. Ask Genzō about the wind.
findings.why: 霧が座る is not an established Japanese expression; it is the English 'the fog sits'. The narration uses the same image (sg.tide_wait 霧が座っていた), so it is a deliberate motif, but in dialogue a listener hears an odd personification, not a dry joke.
findings.direction: If the motif should stay in her mouth, use the idiomatic form, e.g. 霧はまだ居座っています; otherwise 霧はまだ晴れません.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.text: 最後の一通は、灯落の娘宛だった。十年以上口を聞いてない娘に、許してくれって。
findings.en: The last one was to his daughter in Lanternfall. A daughter he hadn't spoken to in over ten years. Asking her to forgive him.
findings.why: 'To be on speaking terms' is 口を利く (or 口をきく); 口を聞く is a common miswriting. The audio is the same, but learners see 聞く 'listen' in the text and its word help.
findings.direction: Write 口を利いてない or 口をきいてない.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 足元を固める言葉ね。今の私に一番必要かも。
findings.en: A word for firm footing. Maybe the one I need most right now.
findings.kansai: 足元を固める言葉やな。今のうちが一番要るもんかも。
findings.why: In the Kansai line, 今のうちが… is first heard as the set phrase 今のうち ('while we still can'), not 'the me of now'. The sentence becomes a garden path for listeners and learners. The standard line is fine.
findings.direction: Reorder so うち is not glued to 今の, e.g. うちに今一番要るもんかも.

findings.speaker: co_ume
findings.text: 小春の頃に甘くなるから、小春。……そう思ってたけど、違うのかもしれないね。実は、生まれた所の名前を借りることがあるから。
findings.en: It sweetens in the koharu days, so it's called Koharu. …That's what I always thought. But maybe not. Fruit sometimes borrows the name of the place it came from.
findings.why: A sentence that opens with 実は、 is read じつは ('actually') by default. The ruby says み, but on screen and to any reader without ruby it is a garden path at the key line of the quest.
findings.direction: Make the noun unambiguous, e.g. 柿の実は、… or 果物は、….

findings.speaker: co_ume
findings.text: ほら、去年の干し柿だ。そのお年寄りに食べさせてごらん。舌は頭より物覚えがいいからね。
findings.en: Here — a dried one from last year. Let the old man taste it. The tongue remembers better than the head.
findings.why: その points back to an old man, but the PC's only line in the scene (#63762c85af) never mentions Yasu or anyone old, so Ume refers to someone she has not been told about. A listener will notice the gap.
findings.direction: Have the PC's question mention the old ferryman who has forgotten the name, or make Ume's reference self-contained, e.g. 名前を忘れた人がいるなら、食べさせてごらん.

findings.speaker: co_asa
findings.text: 雨で流れたんじゃないの。雨なんて降ってないし。朝来たら、真っ白になってた。
findings.en: It didn't wash off — it hasn't even rained. I came up one morning and they were just blank.
findings.why: 〜んじゃないの can mean 'it's not that…' (falling tone) or 'didn't it…?' (rising tone). Read with the common rising tone, Asa contradicts herself in the next sentence.
findings.direction: Either mark falling intonation for the voice actor or remove the ambiguity, e.g. 雨で流れたわけじゃないよ.

findings.speaker: genzo
findings.text: 来な。上を見せてやる。
findings.en: Come on. I'll show you the top.
findings.why: 来な (きな) is the clipped rough imperative 'come'. Learners easily take it for 来るな 'don't come', and Genzō's whole storyline turns on misreading 「来なくていい」 as 「来るな」.
findings.direction: Add a register note: 来な = 来なさい, gruff and friendly, not the negative 来るな. No text change.

findings.speaker: genzo
findings.text: 書けるのか。お前さん。
findings.en: Can you write it? You?
findings.why: お前さん (also sg.ferry_arrives#c463784adb) is an old-fashioned, gruffly warm form of address, not the rude お前 learners are warned about. It is exactly right for Genzō but needs a note.
findings.direction: Register note: お前さん is an older, familiar-but-kindly address; not for learners to copy with strangers.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: さあさあ、お立ち会い！……今日は客が少ないわね。港が静かすぎるのよ。
findings.en: Roll up, roll up! …Thin crowd today. The harbour's too quiet.
findings.why: さあさあ、お立ち会い is a traditional street-performer's call to a crowd (also co.arrive#5a4fcf79a9). It is a set stage phrase that learners cannot parse from お立ち会い's parts.
findings.direction: Register note: a traditional street-performer's call ('gather round'), not used in ordinary speech.

findings.speaker: lq_chigusa
findings.text: あんたには、これを。三十年、卓の上に伏せておいた湯呑みだ。もう要らない。次に借りができた時のために、持っておいき。
findings.en: This is for you. The cup I kept upside down on my table for thirty years. I don't need it now. Keep it for the next time you owe someone.
findings.why: 持っておいき (〜ておいき, an old-style imperative of おく + いく) and her 払わせておくれ (lq.fare_pay#6545e8f633) are older down-to-earth forms that fit her dry voice but are opaque to learners.
findings.direction: Register note: 〜ておいき / 〜ておくれ = older, familiar imperative and request forms (≈ 持っていきなさい / 〜させてください).

findings.speaker: tamae
findings.addressee: pc (regular guests she is fond of)
findings.text: よく寝たかい？朝ご飯は焼き魚だよ。他に何があるってんだ。
findings.en: Sleep well? Breakfast is grilled fish. What else would it be?
findings.why: ってんだ (= というんだ) is a heavy, rough contraction in a rhetorical question, and learners will not find it in a dictionary. The line itself is right for her bustling innkeeper voice.
findings.direction: Word-help or register note: 何があるってんだ = 何があるというのだ, a rough rhetorical 'what else is there?'.

findings.speaker: co_fusa
findings.addressee: pc (guest at her inn who has just helped serve festival orders; friendly)
findings.text: 完璧！数え方がきれいね。杯も個も袋も、一つも間違えないなんて。
findings.en: Perfect! You count beautifully — cups, pieces, bags, not one wrong.
findings.why: The innkeeper lists the counters 杯・個・袋 as if they were nouns, which is the counter lesson's recap coming out of her mouth. Nobody thanks a helper by naming counter suffixes. Aloud, 「はいも、こも、ふくろも」 is close to unintelligible, because 杯 and 個 on their own do not sound like words.
findings.direction: Have her praise the things served or the count itself, and leave the counter recap to the challenge feedback. e.g. 「甘酒も団子も、一つも間違えないなんて」.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: pc (close travelling companion; just before her performance)
findings.text: 見てて。観客一名、最後まで席を立たずにね。
findings.en: Watch me. Audience of one, stay in your seat to the end.
findings.kansai: 見ててな。観客一名、最後まで席を立たんとな。
findings.why: At the end of a Kansai sentence, 〜んとな is the usual 'have to' form (= 〜ないとな). So 「最後まで席を立たんとな」 is heard as 'you'll have to get up by the end', the opposite of the standard 「立たずにね」. It also muddies the callback in co.reflection#a30420ecb9 (「最後まで席を立たず」).
findings.direction: Use the Kansai negative request, so it cannot be read as 'must'. e.g. 「最後まで席立たんといてな」.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: pc (companion), quietly, while the village weeps
findings.text: ……拍手は、しないでおくわ。これは舞台じゃないから。
findings.en: …I won't applaud. This isn't a stage.
findings.kansai: ……拍手は、せえへんでおくわ。これは舞台ちゃうから。
findings.why: 「せえへんでおく」 maps しないでおく word for word, and Kansai speakers do not say it. The natural form is せんとく(わ) or やめとくわ. This is the chapter's climax line, so the made-up form will stand out to a Kansai listener. The standard line is fine.
findings.direction: Use the contracted Kansai 'deliberately not do' form. e.g. 「……拍手は、せんとくわ。これは舞台ちゃうから」.

findings.speaker: co_tomoe
findings.addressee: Hiro (her small son), in a memory of the fire night
findings.text: いい、今はいい。……ヒロ、おいで。頭にこれを巻いておきな。火の粉が熱いからね。
findings.en: Never mind — not now. …Hiro, come here. Tie this round your head. The sparks are hot.
findings.why: 「巻いておきな」 is the clipped なさい imperative (masu-stem + な): a warm command from a parent or elder. The word help for な covers casual emphasis, and prohibition after the dictionary form, so a learner can easily take it as 巻いておくな ('don't tie it'). Suzu repeats the phrase as the scene's emotional hook (co.core_page#bfe25bca65), so the meaning matters.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note: verb stem + な = soft command (short for 〜なさい), said by parents and elders to children; contrast it with the dictionary form + な (巻くな = don't).

findings.speaker: co_goro
findings.text: 旅の人、一つ頼まれてくれんか。丈夫な綱を、一本探してきてほしい。
findings.en: Traveller, would you do me a favour? Find me one good strong rope.
findings.why: 「頼まれてくれる」 (passive + くれる, 'take on a request for me') is an idiomatic, folksy way to ask a favour. With the 〜ん negative it is opaque to a learner, who will parse it as a passive 'be asked'. It comes back at co.goro#90e0d439a5 (「最初に頼まれてくれたのはあんただ」).
findings.direction: No text change. Add a note that 頼まれてくれ(ん)か = 'would you do me a favour?' (older, homely), with ん = ない.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.text: 鐘の話、聞いたか。皆、鐘が鳴ったら水路へ走ったって。頭が忘れても、足が道を覚えてた。
findings.en: Heard about the bell? Everyone ran to the channel when it rang. Their heads forgot; their feet remembered the way.
findings.why: Banter 4 plays after the kiln whether or not the optional bell quest happened. If it did (co_bell_rung), the player was standing there and Nao already said 「見たか。全員、迷わず水路に走った」 at co.bell_ring, so retelling it as hearsay (〜って) to someone who saw it is odd. If it did not, there is no ringing to have heard about.
findings.direction: Make the line depend on co_bell_rung and recast it as a shared memory, with a different opener otherwise. e.g. 「さっきの鐘、見たろ。頭が忘れても、足が道を覚えてた」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc (close companion; tender moment after the player says 'we get lost together')
findings.text: ……それは、旅に出る時に私が約束したことです。言い返されたのは、初めてですね。
findings.en: …That's the promise I made when we set out. It's the first time anyone has said it back to me.
findings.why: 「言い返す」 mainly means to retort or talk back in an argument. It is a literal take on 'said it back to me', so this moved, surprised moment sounds as if Ren has been contradicted.
findings.direction: Say 'had my own words given back to me'. Keep Ren's polite register. e.g. 「同じ言葉を返してもらったのは、初めてです」.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: Hiro (adult craftsman, a stranger at first meeting)
findings.text: 額の手拭い、汗止めですね。火の粉除けにもなる。賢い。
findings.en: The cloth on your forehead — for sweat. And to keep sparks off, too. Smart.
findings.why: A bare 「賢い」 said to an adult stranger's face is the kind of grading praise you give a child or a pupil. It clashes with Mio's polite manner toward strangers, and with her own anger at being talked down to (co.b_mio3).
findings.direction: Praise the idea rather than the person, or keep it polite. e.g. 「よく考えてありますね」.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion), aside, while the whole square weeps
findings.text: 皆さん、泣いています。……薬で止めてはいけない涙ですね。
findings.en: Everyone's crying. …These are tears no medicine should stop.
findings.why: Mio is speaking to the player, but 「皆さん、」 with a comma at the start of the sentence is the standard way to address a crowd. Aloud it can sound as if she is telling the crowd 'Everyone, you are crying'. The same opener is at co.bell_ring#2fa784b71e.
findings.direction: Make 皆さん the subject, not a form of address: add が, or give the actors a note to read it as a hushed aside. e.g. 「皆さんが、泣いています」.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion), about the villagers at the channel
findings.text: 皆さん、息が上がっている。怖かったんです。理由も分からないまま……
findings.en: They're all out of breath. They were frightened — without knowing why…
findings.why: This has the same vocative-sounding 「皆さん、」 opener as co.assembly#ac04a84672. Here an honorific subject is followed by a plain 〜ている predicate, which makes it sound even more like she is addressing the crowd.
findings.direction: Same fix as the assembly line. e.g. 「皆さんの息が上がっています」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc and Kotarō (a child), about the mixed-up order
findings.text: 助数詞一つで、皿が徳利になる。言葉は恐ろしい。美しい。
findings.en: One counter word, and plates become flasks. Language is terrifying. And beautiful.
findings.why: 「助数詞」 is grammar-lesson vocabulary. Everyone else in this storyline says 数え方 (the PC, Nobu, Fusa), and Ren says it in front of a child, so the lesson seems to be speaking through Ren. The same term is at co.pottery_slip#0edfa27a02. Ren's precision could justify using it once, so this is Robin's call.
findings.direction: Use the everyday word in at least one of the two lines, and keep the deadpan pair 「恐ろしい。美しい。」. e.g. 「数え方一つで、皿が徳利になる」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc (companion), at the climax of the assembly
findings.text: 名が灯りました。……師匠は、言わない名は薄くなる、と言っていました。今夜、五つの名が濃くなった。
findings.en: The names are lit. …My master used to say that a name nobody speaks grows thin. Tonight, five names grew dark again.
findings.why: In co.b_ren2#a7f2069713 Ren quotes the master word for word: 「口に出さない名は、薄くなる」. At the climax the same saying comes back as 「言わない名は薄くなる」. Precise Ren would quote it the same way, and the echo is the point of the line.
findings.direction: Use one wording for the saying in both places (the banter's 口に出さない名 is the stronger one).

findings.speaker: co_kotaro
findings.text: 白いヤギがまた逃げた！……僕が追いかけているんじゃないよ。ヤギが先に走るんだ。
findings.en: The white goat got out again! …I'm not chasing it. It runs first!
findings.why: Everywhere else Kotarō contracts (してる, 怒ってる, 分かってる). The uncontracted 「追いかけている」 in an excited shout sounds read aloud from a page, and so does 「見ているだけなら」 in co.lw_sl_co_kotaro_r3#ac279d4c62. Both lines come from the living-world file (src/content/zzz_living/40_co.js).
findings.direction: Contract both to match his other lines: 「追いかけてるんじゃないよ」 and 「見てるだけなら」.

findings.speaker: co_asa
findings.text: 道しるべの火除け道の腕、今朝皆が見上げて歩いてたよ。
findings.en: This morning everyone was looking up at the "firebreak path" arm as they walked.
findings.why: The chain of three の, 「道しるべの火除け道の腕」, is hard to follow aloud. The listener cannot hear that 火除け道 is the label painted on the arm (the English needs quotation marks for the same reason).
findings.direction: Split the sentence or mark the label. e.g. 「道しるべに『火除け道』の腕がついたでしょ。今朝、みんな見上げて歩いてたよ」.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: Hiro (near-stranger to him; she is hiding that she knows him)
findings.text: ……素敵な習わしね。ありがとう、話してくれて。
findings.en: …It's a lovely custom. Thank you for telling us.
findings.kansai: ……素敵な習わしですね。ありがとう、話してくれはって。
findings.why: The standard line is plain (〜ね, 話してくれて). The Kansai version adds です and an honorific はる on Hiro's own action (話してくれはって), so the dialect setting changes how politely she speaks to Hiro. Her next line to him (旅芸人の顔は…見た顔よ / やで) is plain in both versions.
findings.direction: Keep the same politeness in both versions. Plain fits her breezy cover with Hiro, so drop the です/はる from the Kansai line. e.g. ……素敵な習わしやね。ありがとう、話してくれて。

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 私、甘酒には目がないの。知ってた？
findings.en: I have a weakness for amazake. Did you know?
findings.kansai: うち、甘酒には目があらへんねん。知ってた？
findings.why: 〜に目がない is a fixed idiom ('can't resist'). The Kansai conversion turns the ない into あらへん, which breaks the idiom: 目があらへん sounds like a literal 'I have no eyes', or a botched idiom. Kansai speakers keep 目がない as it is.
findings.direction: Keep the idiom intact in the Kansai line and put the dialect in the ending. e.g. うち、甘酒には目ぇないねん。

findings.speaker: hiro
findings.addressee: pc (outsider who just spoke up for Suzu), about Suzu
findings.text: 分かってる。二十年遅れでも、来た。……それは数える。
findings.en: I know. Twenty years late, but she came. …That counts.
findings.why: それは数える is a word-for-word calque of English 'that counts'. 数える does not mean 'matters / is acknowledged' in Japanese, so the payoff line of the scene would sound odd to a native listener.
findings.direction: Use a Japanese way of saying 'I'll give her credit for that', ideally one that keeps the ledger motif. e.g. ……それは、勘定に入れとく。

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: Ume (elderly villager, met once, has just recalled leading children out of the fire), in her presence
findings.text: 子どもを連れて逃げたのは、ばあさんだったのか。水路が逃げ道。石に彫ってあったとおりだ。
findings.en: So it was you who led the children out. Down the channel — just like the stone says.
findings.why: Calling a kind elderly woman ばあさん to her face, right after she has shared a painful memory, sounds rude rather than wry. It also clashes with Nao's only polite question in the game, which is put to her in co.ume_first (梁は、どこから持ってきたものですか). Nao saying 婆さん about third parties elsewhere is fine.
findings.direction: Keep Nao plain but address her by name or with Nao's usual あんた. e.g. 子どもを連れて逃げたのは、ウメさんだったのか。

findings.speaker: co_tokiwa
findings.text: ……鐘を外せと言ったこと、ゴロウさんに謝りました。笑われましたよ。腕の方が頭より賢い、と。
findings.en: …I apologised to Gorō for telling him to take the rope down. He laughed at me. Said arms are wiser than heads.
findings.why: In co.bell_ring Tokiwa shouted 綱を外してください (take the rope down), and the English here says 'rope'. The Japanese says 鐘 (the bell), so the recorded line would contradict the scene it refers to.
findings.direction: Change 鐘 to 綱 so it matches co.bell_ring and the English. The plain quoted imperative (外せと) is fine.

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: 一つは朝の合図だったみたいだよ。帳面を思い出そう。
findings.en: One stroke seems to have been the morning signal. Let's remember the notebook.
findings.why: This is a real ?(comp) line with no branch by companion (confirmed in src/content/ch4/30_scenes_hamlet.js), so Ren may say it. Ren never uses friendly plain だよ to the player anywhere in the game. Also, 帳面を思い出そう ('remember the notebook') is a slightly odd object: it is the rules in the notebook that need remembering.
findings.direction: Either split by companion (as the :two branch already does) or use wording that suits all four voices. e.g. 一つは朝の合図だったはず。帳面の決まり、思い出して。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: 三つは夕方のヤギの合図だね。今は昼だよ。
findings.en: Three is the evening goat signal. It's noon now.
findings.why: Any companion may say this (the source already branches the gestures by companion but not the line). だね…だよ suits Nao, Suzu and plain-mode Mio, but it is clearly off for Ren, who would say ですね / ですよ.
findings.direction: Give Ren (or each companion) their own line, as the gesture lines already do, or use a register-neutral fragment. e.g. 三つは、夕方のヤギの合図。今は昼。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: ……吹雪の合図だよ、それ。みんなに謝りに行かないと。
findings.en: …That's the storm signal. We'll have to go round and apologise to everyone.
findings.why: This is a generic ?(comp) line. The dislocated, casual 〜だよ、それ。 fits Nao or Suzu and would sound out of character from Ren.
findings.direction: Split by companion or neutralise the ending. e.g. ……今のは、吹雪の合図。皆に謝りに行かないと。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: 日誌は、あの大きな机の上だね。
findings.en: The log is on that big table.
findings.why: This {if comp} line comes after the companion-specific lines and has no condition, so Ren can say it. 〜だね is not in Ren's voice.
findings.direction: Use a register-neutral hint or one line per companion. e.g. 日誌は、あの大きな机の上。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: 鍵が要る。机の上の書き置きに、何か書いてない？
findings.en: We need a key. Doesn't the note on the desk say something?
findings.why: This is a generic line. The casual question 書いてない？ fits Nao, Suzu or Mio, but not Ren, who would ask 書いてありませんか.
findings.direction: Neutralise, or vary by companion. e.g. 鍵が要る。机の上の書き置きに、何か書いてあるかも。

findings.speaker: any
findings.addressee: pc (companion; condition comp!=mio, so Nao, Ren or Suzu)
findings.text: 少し休もう。あのストーブ、使えるかもしれない。
findings.en: Let's rest a bit. That stove might still work.
findings.why: Mio gets her own polite line here, but Ren falls into this plain one, and plain volitional 休もう is not how Ren suggests things (Ren says 行きましょう / 書き直しましょう).
findings.direction: Add a Ren line as was done for Mio, or make the fall-through neutral. e.g. あのストーブ、まだ使えるかもしれない。少し休める。

findings.speaker: hiro
findings.text: 他に何か理由がある気がするんだが、考えると頭が白くなる。
findings.en: I feel there's some other reason, but when I try to think about it, my head goes white.
findings.why: The idiom for 'my mind goes blank' is 頭が真っ白になる. Without 真っ, 頭が白くなる reads first as 'my hair turns white'. The echo of the game's 'fading white' motif is clearly deliberate, but the line sounds slightly off aloud.
findings.direction: Keep the motif with the idiomatic form. e.g. 考えると、頭が真っ白になる。

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: Shino (post clerk, polite acquaintance) / pc, light banter
findings.text: 同感だ。宛名なんて、手紙の一番外側にすぎない。
findings.en: Agreed. The address is just the outermost part of a letter.
findings.why: 〜にすぎない is written or formal in tone (the game's own grammar note adv_ni_suginai says so), and 同感だ is stiff. Together they turn a wry Nao quip into an essay sentence.
findings.direction: Keep the thought but say it in Nao's spoken register. e.g. だな。宛名なんて、手紙の一番外っ側だ。

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: Hiro (the boy she lied to twenty years ago; confession)
findings.text: 私はそれを知っていて、春に帰るって言った。慰めのつもりだった。でもそれは、君から泣く時間を取り上げた。
findings.en: I knew, and I told you she'd be back in spring. I meant it as comfort. But it took away your time to cry.
findings.why: In the last sentence an inanimate subject (それ, the lie) takes away 'time to cry' from you, which follows the English sentence shape and sounds written in a halting spoken confession. 君 to Hiro (twice in this scene) is Suzu's only use of it with a peer. It may be deliberate (the big-sister view of a seven-year-old), but it should be a conscious choice. The Kansai line uses あんた.
findings.direction: Make the last clause speech-shaped and confirm the pronoun choice. e.g. でもそのせいで、君は泣くこともできなかった。

findings.speaker: hiro
findings.text: 席は、今年も空けておく。でも今年は、母の名前を書く。帰ってくる人の席じゃない。覚えている人の席だ。
findings.en: I'll keep the seat free this year too. But this year I'll write her name on it. Not a seat for someone coming back. A seat for someone remembered.
findings.why: Parallel to 帰ってくる人 ('the person who comes back'), 覚えている人 most naturally reads as 'the person who remembers', not 'the person we remember'. Aloud, the key line of the scene can flip its meaning.
findings.direction: Make it unambiguous that the seat is for remembering her, not for 'a person who remembers'. e.g. 帰ってくる人の席じゃない。覚えておくための席だ。

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 衣装を食べるのはやめて！昔、それで幕を一枚失ったんだから！
findings.en: Don't eat the costume! I lost a whole curtain to one of you once!
findings.kansai: 衣装食べるのはやめて！昔、それで幕を一枚失ってんから！
findings.why: 失った is a written or solemn verb for 'lost'. In a squawked comic line people say 食べられた / ダメにされた. The Kansai 失ってんから is stiffer still.
findings.direction: Use a colloquial verb in both versions. e.g. 昔、それで幕を一枚食べられたんだから！

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: さあさあ、雪の舞台の幕開けだよ！……さむっ。客席に火鉢をください。
findings.en: Roll up, roll up — the curtain rises on the snow stage! …Brr. Braziers for the audience, please.
findings.kansai: さあさあ、雪の舞台の幕開けやで！……さむっ。客席に火鉢ちょうだい。
findings.why: The standard line ends with a mock-polite stage request (火鉢をください), but the Kansai version turns it into casual ちょうだい. The joke's register shifts with the dialect setting. It is minor, but it is exactly the polite/dialect split the brief asks to keep.
findings.direction: Keep the mock-polite request in Kansai too (ください works in Kansai). Alternatively, make both versions casual.

findings.speaker: co_ume
findings.text: おや、旅の人。段々畑は初めてかい。坂が急だから、足元に気をお付け。
findings.en: Well now, travellers. First time on the terraces? The slopes are steep — mind your feet.
findings.why: お + stem as a soft command (気をお付け, and later 持ってお行き / 見てご覧 in co.ume) is an old-fashioned, motherly elder form. Neither the grammar notes nor the lexicon cover it, and learners will not know it is not a polite form.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a register note for お+stem imperatives (elderly or motherly, warm, not for learners' own use with superiors).

findings.speaker: hoshino
findings.addressee: pc and companion (younger helpers he is grateful to)
findings.text: もう少し、ここで灯りを見ているよ。先に下りておくれ。
findings.en: I'll watch the lamp a little longer. Go on down ahead of me.
findings.why: 〜ておくれ is a marked elder request form, also used by Fuki (勘弁しておくれ, 覚えておいておくれ). No lexicon or grammar entry covers it, and learners may misparse it as 遅れ ('be late'), which is the only おくれ in the lexicon.
findings.direction: No text change. Add a word-help or register note: 〜ておくれ = older, familiar form of 〜てくれ / 〜てください, used by elders.

findings.speaker: hiro
findings.text: あんたが行っちまったことに、だ。母は一座と行った、と聞いた。それから一座も、あんたも行った。俺は二人分、待ってたんだ。
findings.en: It's that you left. I was told my mother went with the troupe. Then the troupe left, and you with it. I was waiting for two people.
findings.why: 〜ちまう (rougher or older form of 〜ちゃう / 〜てしまう) appears here at an emotional peak and again with Fuki (なっちまった, 帰ってきちまう). The casual_contractions note lists 〜ちゃう but not 〜ちまう.
findings.direction: No text change. Add 〜ちまう / 〜ちまった to the contraction note (= 〜てしまう; rough or old-fashioned colouring).

findings.speaker: any
findings.addressee: pc (companion, mid-journey; urgent call to run for the bell)
findings.text: $name、鐘の決まり、覚えてるよね？行こう！
findings.en: $name, you remember the bell rules, right? Let's go!
findings.kansai: $name、鐘の決まり、覚えてるやろ？行こ！
findings.why: The source gate is ?(comp), with no branch, so all four companions say it. Ren speaks to the player in です/ます through the whole chapter, and Mio's chapter-4 lines to the player in public are also polite (e.g. みんな、聞こえたみたいです。行きましょう、わたしたちも。 two lines later). Casual 覚えてるよね？行こう！ is out of voice for both. Nao would rather say よな.
findings.direction: Split by companion, as the reaction lines just after it already are, or write a neutral fragment all four can say; e.g. Ren: 鐘の決まり、覚えていますね。行きましょう。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: 扉の鍵はホシノさんが持っているはずです。先に話を聞きましょう。
findings.en: Hoshino should have the key to the door. Let's talk to him first.
findings.kansai: 扉の鍵はホシノさんが持ってはるはずや。先に話聞こ。
findings.why: The gate is ?(sb_morning&!sb_obs_open), with no companion condition, so Nao and Suzu say this careful です/ましょう line to the player. Nao has about 2 polite lines in the whole game. The Kansai pass had to turn it casual (持ってはるはずや。先に話聞こ。) to make it work for Suzu, which shows the standard line does not fit her.
findings.direction: Give Nao and Suzu their own lines, or make the shared line a register-neutral fragment; e.g. 鍵はホシノさんのところ……先に話を。

findings.speaker: any
findings.text: デンジさんの言っていた、裏の階段でしょうか。中から開けられるはずです。
findings.en: That must be the back stair Denji mentioned. It should open from inside.
findings.kansai: デンジさんが言わはった、裏の階段ちゃうか。中から開けられるはずやで。
findings.why: The gate is ?(comp!=nao), so Mio, Ren and Suzu say it. In standard mode Suzu would say でしょうか…はずです to the player, which is not her voice (about 5 polite lines in the game). The Kansai version is casual (ちゃうか…はずやで), so the same speaker's politeness also differs between standard and dialect.
findings.direction: Add a Suzu-specific line (casual in standard, matching the existing Kansai one), or make the shared line neutral; e.g. Suzu: デンジさんの言ってた裏の階段かな。中から開くはずだよ。

findings.speaker: nao
findings.text: ……今の、聞いたか。頼んだぞ。三十年ぶりに。
findings.en: …Did you hear that? Kasane asked. First time in thirty years.
findings.why: Said on its own with no subject, 頼んだぞ is the set phrase 'I'm counting on you'. A listener hears Nao handing the job to the player, not reporting that Kasane asked for something. The point of the scene (Kasane asking for the first time) is lost aloud.
findings.direction: Make it clear the line reports Kasane's request (subject or 人に/頼みごと); e.g. あいつが人に頼んだぞ。三十年ぶりに。

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: pc (close companion), after the charter puzzle
findings.text: 「もし」は「もし」だ。「だけ」を足したのはカサネだ。
findings.en: "If" means "if". Kasane's the one who added "only".
findings.why: The Japanese plaque (求められれば、返す) and Kasane's note (求められなければ、返さなくてよい) contain neither もし nor だけ. The line follows the English lesson's 'if / only if' wording, so it quotes words the player never saw.
findings.direction: Quote the forms actually on screen; e.g. 「求められれば」は「求められたときだけ」じゃない。そう読んだのはカサネだ。

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: Hoshino (elderly stranger who has written letters for years) and pc
findings.text: 宛名は、手紙の行き先の名前です。灯りの名前と同じように、持っていかれたのでしょう。
findings.en: An address is the name of where a letter is going. It must have been taken, just like a lamp's name.
findings.why: Ren gives a dictionary definition of 宛名 to an old man who has just described his own letters coming back blank. It reads as a teaching gloss leaking into the scene, not Ren's precise link-making.
findings.direction: Keep the insight (address = a name, so it was taken like the lamp's) and drop the definition; e.g. 宛名も、名前ですから。灯りの名前と同じように……。

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc (companion) in an emergency, the hearth dying and the children freezing
findings.text: $name、「ほのお」です。灯守が最初に習う字の一つ。わたしが形を示します。あなたが書いてください。
findings.en: $name — "honoo", flame. One of the first words a keeper learns. I'll show you the shape; you write it.
findings.why: Four full sentences in a crisis, including a piece of keeper trivia. The explicit わたしが…あなたが… contrast and written-register 示します follow the English 'I'll show you; you write it'. Even careful Ren would compress this.
findings.direction: Shorter and urgent, keeping Ren's politeness and dropping the pronoun pair and the trivia; e.g. 「ほのお」です。形は見せます。書いてください。

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc (companion), looking at Akari's height notches
findings.text: 記録ですね。一番美しい種類の。
findings.en: A record. The most beautiful kind.
findings.why: Putting 一番美しい種類の after the noun copies 'the most beautiful kind'. Spoken Japanese does not add a 種類の phrase after the noun like this.
findings.direction: Keep the sentiment, Japanese order; e.g. いちばん美しい記録です。

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: 上の大きな灯りが戻れば、これらも戻るでしょう。灯りは、互いの名前を呼び合っているものです。
findings.en: If the great lamp above comes back, these will too. Lamps call each other's names.
findings.why: これら is written or presentation register. In speech, pointing at the stair lanterns, even formal speakers say ここの灯りも / この灯りたちも. It sounds translated, not careful.
findings.direction: Replace これら with a spoken deictic; e.g. 石段の灯りも戻るでしょう。

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: 建物が動いていると考えることにしました。そのほうが、精神にいい。
findings.en: I've decided the building is moving. It's better for my peace of mind.
findings.why: 精神にいい copies 'good for my mind/peace of mind'. The fixed phrase is 精神衛生上いい (or 気が楽です), and using the fixed phrase would make Ren's deadpan land harder.
findings.direction: Use the idiom; e.g. そのほうが、精神衛生上いい。

findings.speaker: yae
findings.addressee: pc (guest, stopping them at the door in a storm)
findings.text: だめだめ！吹雪の夜に外に出るのは、雪鈴でいちばんの禁止事項だよ！
findings.en: No, no! Going outside on a storm night is the number one rule in Snowbell!
findings.why: 禁止事項 is notice-board or regulation vocabulary. In the mouth of a warm, bossy innkeeper shouting at a guest it sounds like official phrasing, and いちばんの禁止事項 also follows the English 'number one rule'.
findings.direction: Everyday wording; e.g. 吹雪の夜に外に出るのは、雪鈴じゃいちばんやっちゃいけないことだよ！

findings.speaker: kanta
findings.text: ここから天文台の灯りがいちばんよく見えるんだ。ホシノじいちゃんの望遠鏡、ちょっとだけ借りている。
findings.en: You can see the observatory lamp best from here. I'm borrowing Grandpa Hoshino's telescope. Just a bit.
findings.why: An excited boy using full 〜ている in casual chat sounds like reading aloud. Kanta contracts in his main lines (ともしてるんだ, 習ってるんだ). The same living-world file has 魚を待っているんだ (r3), and Sachi's 長くなってしまった (r3) is similarly unreduced.
findings.direction: Contract to match his other lines (借りてる, 待ってるんだ); word help for 〜てる is already common.

findings.speaker: natsume
findings.text: 子ヤギの番。……寝てないよ。目を閉じて数えているだけ。
findings.en: Minding the kids. …I'm not asleep. Just counting with my eyes shut.
findings.why: Within one drowsy line she contracts (寝てない) and then switches to the full 数えている. A sleepy teen would say 数えてるだけ. r3 has the same issue: ヤギを数えているの.
findings.direction: Contract consistently; e.g. 目、閉じて数えてるだけ。

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: ……あんたの名前もあるよ。結構長くなってきた。困ったもんだね。
findings.en: …Your name's in there too. It's getting rather long. What a problem.
findings.kansai: ……あんたの名前もあるで。結構長くなってきたわ。困ったもんやな。
findings.why: In standard Japanese, Suzu calls the player あなた everywhere else (co, pages, road, endings, sa2.end_suzu); あんた appears only here and once in lq. In Kansai あんた is natural, but in the standard line it suddenly sounds rougher, at the tenderest moment of her scene.
findings.direction: Decide if this is an intentional intimacy shift. If not, use あなた (or the name) in standard and keep あんた in KANSAI.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 幕代で一座は赤字になったけどね。帳簿はあたしがつけてたから、よく覚えてる。一枚八百。
findings.en: The curtains put the troupe in the red. I kept the books, so I remember exactly. Eight hundred a curtain.
findings.why: Suzu's standard first person is わたし/私 across the game, including this part's ch6 lines (sa.b_suzu3 わたしも、ヒロに…; sa.choose_kasane 帳簿はわたしが付ける). Chapter 4 alone switches to あたし (sb.inn_menu#d9cd7f3d3a, sb.tetsuji#cfd3d2a80e, sb.quiet_suzu#4eedb84845, #7a0a1e886f, #2aa9265f86). Her actor would change first-person pronoun by chapter.
findings.direction: Choose one standard pronoun for Suzu. Or, if あたし is meant as her off-stage or ledger voice, apply that rule consistently across chapters.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 舞台を降りて、客席の娘さんに会いに行く。……最高の終幕じゃない。
findings.en: Stepping down off the stage to meet your daughter in the audience. …What a finale.
findings.why: This is the affirmative exclamation じゃない ('isn't that the best finale'), but ending in 。 it reads on the page, and to TTS, as negation ('it's not the best finale'). The actor needs the right emphatic intonation, and a learner tapping じゃない gets the negative.
findings.direction: Mark the intonation with punctuation (じゃない！ or じゃない？) or use じゃん; optionally a register note on affirmative じゃない.

findings.speaker: fuki
findings.addressee: pc (young traveller who rang the bell)
findings.text: 吹雪の鐘、あんたが鳴らしたね。音でわかる。若い腕の音だ。……悪くなかったよ。
findings.en: You rang the storm bell. I could tell by the sound. Young arms. …Not bad at all.
findings.why: The player has just heard Fuki in sb.storm_start#cacfa69aac: 吹雪の鐘を鳴らしたのは、あんたかい。若い腕の音だった。 When they talk to her minutes later, she works it out again in nearly the same words, as if they had not just spoken.
findings.direction: Make the residents line follow on from the storm_start exchange (e.g. thanks, or a dry comment on technique) instead of repeating the deduction.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (companion; the morning after Mio's private night talk)
findings.text: あの目……熱のある子の目に似ています。苦しいのかもしれない。
findings.en: Those eyes… they look like a feverish child's. Maybe it's suffering.
findings.why: Mio is polite to the player in chapter 4 public lines and softens to plain in sb.quiet_mio and sb.quiet_morning. The next morning's observatory lines go back to です/ます (this line; sb.path_bench#b3c3bbcad4 測っていたんですね; sb.stair_ice#904c39e198 凍りますから; and in other parts hall_enter, charts_stove…). Then from chapter 5 she is plain. So the night's turning point is undone for one dungeon.
findings.direction: Robin's call where the softening lands. If the night talk is the turning point, move post-night lines to the player toward soft plain (keep polite to Hoshino); e.g. 熱のある子の目に似てる。

findings.speaker: tetsuji
findings.text: 子ヤギは母親にくっついて寝ている。吹雪も知らんで。……うらやましい。
findings.en: The kids are asleep curled against their mother. Don't even know there's a storm. …Lucky things.
findings.why: Tetsuji's other ん-negatives (おけん, いかん, 名乗り出ん) read as gruff role speech. 知らんで meaning 'without knowing' is a western-dialect form, though, and in this game Kansai 知らんで is Suzu's 'I don't know, y'know'. Word help maps 知らん to 知る, so the negation disappears for learners.
findings.direction: Keep his gruffness but use a standard connective; e.g. 吹雪も知らずに。

findings.speaker: tetsuji
findings.text: ヤギは小屋に入れた。十二頭、全部な。他人のヤギでも、吹雪に放ってはおけん。
findings.en: The goats are in the shed. All twelve. Somebody else's or not, you don't leave a goat out in a storm.
findings.why: The gruff negative 〜ん = 〜ない runs through Tetsuji's and Denji's lines (おけん, 返さないといかん, 名乗り出ん, Denji's 開かん). Word help maps 名乗り出ん to 名乗り出る and 開かん to 開く with no note that the form is negative. A learner can read the opposite meaning.
findings.direction: Add a register note on first meeting: 〜ん = 〜ない (gruff/older plain speech), plus いかん = いけない. No text change.

findings.speaker: hoshino
findings.addressee: pc and companion (younger visitors he trusts)
findings.text: 石段はとけたかね。わたしも支度をしているところだ。先に行っておくれ。灯りの前で会おう。
findings.en: Has the stair melted? I'm getting ready myself. Go on ahead. We'll meet at the lamp.
findings.why: Hoshino uses 〜ておくれ five times (also 書いておくれ, 伝えておくれ, 声をかけておくれ ×2), together with かね and かい. It is a fitting, gentle elderly voice, but おくれ is a dated request form. It is not in the lexicon, and the kana could be mistaken for 遅れる.
findings.direction: Keep the text. Add a register note: 〜ておくれ = 〜てくれ, older and gentle.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.text: 今夜の話は、宛名なしであんたに預けておく。誰にも届けんなよ。
findings.en: Tonight's talk I'm leaving with you, no address on it. Don't go delivering it to anyone.
findings.why: The source tags 届けんな@届ける, so word help shows only 'to deliver' and loses the prohibitive 〜んな (= 〜るな). A learner can read 'I'll deliver it to everyone', the opposite of the line's tender point.
findings.direction: No text change. Gloss 届けんな as 届けるな, rough casual 'don't'.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (closest companion, end of the journey; same ending scene in which she has just been speaking soft plain to them)
findings.text: これは、そのまま。決めていないことの場所です。……中身は、だいぶ減りました。
findings.en: That one stays as it is. A place for what I haven't decided yet. …There's a lot less in it now.
findings.why: sa2.end_mio is called from end.mio.c inside sa.end_comp, moments after Mio speaks plain to the player (見て。新しい札。／持ってて。／嬉しそうな顔、しないでよ。／end.mio.b: お茶は交代で淹れよう。今週はあなた。). Every line of sa2.end_mio switches to です/ます (also #c19a85b8dc, #b47e6ba7a5, #26f7d7c013, #3f8cf4bf1d) with no emotional or situational trigger, so she sounds as if she were explaining her shelves to a customer.
findings.direction: Put the whole sa2.end_mio block into the soft plain she uses in the rest of the ending, keeping the content. Illustrative only: 'これは、そのまま。決めてないことの場所。……中身は、だいぶ減ったよ。'

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (close companion who has just called her name; ch6 Archive gate)
findings.text: ……聞こえました。名前を呼んでもらうと、声って戻るんですね。薬には、できないことです。
findings.en: …I heard it. When someone calls your name, your voice comes back. That's something no medicine can do.
findings.why: At the Archive gate Mio is plain to the player in every adjacent line (sa.gate_first 水の中に、字が見える。…運ばれてるんだ。; sa.hut_register_signed, sa.heart_enter). Here she gives a three-sentence polite reflection to the friend who just called her name, while the other three companions keep their usual register. Polite could be read as being shaken, but the content is reflective, not startled.
findings.direction: Use plain, or at most one stunned polite word and then plain. Illustrative only: '……聞こえた。名前を呼んでもらうと、声って戻るんだね。'

findings.speaker: mio
findings.addressee: pc (closest companion / romantic partner, end of the journey)
findings.text: ……はい。手、温かいですね。今日は、薬の匂いがしない。
findings.en: …Yes. Your hand's warm. And today it doesn't smell of medicine.
findings.why: This is called from end.mio.c straight after her plain ending lines, and all three branch replies are polite (also #0705cc94a8 私も、そうしたかったです。, #8e10fae789 一番安心します。). A shy ……はい can work as an acceptance, but sustained です/ます to the person she has been speaking plain with makes the closest moment sound more distant than the rest of the ending.
findings.direction: Keep the shy ……はい if Robin wants a flustered beat, but let the rest fall back into her soft plain. Illustrative only: '……うん。手、温かいね。今日は、薬の匂いがしない。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.text: 字が好きなんですね。
findings.en: You really like handwriting.
findings.why: In companion banter the PC is plain everywhere else (sg.arrive それ、褒めてる？; co.b_nao2 その手紙、まだ持っているの？; sa.b_nao1 ナオは、変わったね。). Only the Lanternfall (ch5) banter turns the PC polite. To Nao, the least ceremonious companion, 〜んですね sounds like a stranger. Nothing in the scene marks it as the town's over-politeness rubbing off.
findings.direction: Make it plain like the PC's other banter. Illustrative only: '字が好きなんだね。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.text: ミオも、よく「大丈夫」と言いますよね。
findings.en: You say "I'm fine" a lot too, Mio.
findings.why: This has the same ch5-only PC politeness toward a companion (compare co.b_mio2 断ってもよかったんだよ。, sa.b_mio2 何をしてるの？). Mio's own reply ……気をつけます。 works as her sheepish formal answer either way, so it can stay.
findings.direction: Make the PC line plain. Illustrative only: 'ミオも、よく「大丈夫」って言うよね。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.text: 厳しいですね。
findings.en: That's strict.
findings.why: This has the same ch5-only PC politeness toward a companion (compare co.b_suzu1 踏んでくればいいのに。). Suzu answers in her usual plain, so the exchange sounds lopsided.
findings.direction: Make it plain. Illustrative only: '厳しいね。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.addressee: the travelling companion (any of the four), on arrival
findings.text: 下りてみましょう。
findings.en: Let's go down.
findings.why: The line answers the companion's arrival chatter. The other chapter arrivals have the PC plain to the companion (co.arrive 祭りの前に着いたみたいだね。; sg.arrive それ、褒めてる？), so the polite volitional is the same ch5 drift.
findings.direction: Use the plain volitional. Illustrative only: '下りてみよう。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.text: 鳴らしたのは、トウヤという人です。使いの。鍵を持って、自分で開けた。
findings.en: The one who rang it was named Tōya. The messenger. He had the key, and he opened it himself.
findings.why: To an elderly stranger the PC opens politely (トウヤという人です) and then ends on a bare plain 自分で開けた. It reads as a slip rather than a deliberate shift. The 使いの fragment is fine.
findings.direction: Keep the polite frame through the final sentence. Illustrative only: '…鍵を持って、自分で開けたんです。'

findings.speaker: pc
findings.addressee: Akari (records clerk, met and named; polite acquaintance)
findings.text: 洪水の年の台帳を写したのは、あなたですか。
findings.en: Was it you who copied the ledger for the flood year?
findings.why: The PC knows Akari's name (she introduces herself in lf.akari) but calls her あなた here and in lf.akari_letters#b3940d359d (あなたを待っていますよ). Using あなた repeatedly to a named person is English-shaped, and 写したのは、あなたですか sounds accusatory to a nervous clerk. The あなた inside Hoshino's reported request in lf.akari_reply#e538a2d307 is fine.
findings.direction: Use her name or drop the pronoun. Illustrative only: '洪水の年の台帳を写したのは、アカリさんですか。'

findings.speaker: umi
findings.addressee: Nao (the courier who delivered her father's letter; guarded but grateful)
findings.text: 決めなくていいって、あんた言ったよね。
findings.en: You said I didn't have to decide.
findings.why: This is Umi's only あんた in the game. With Nao she has used ナオさん (lf.umi_after#0e431b76de ……ナオさん。返事、ちゃんと届けてね。) or no pronoun at all (lf.nao_deliver). あんた is blunter than her controlled, dignified voice and than the relationship as last shown.
findings.direction: Drop the pronoun or use her established address. Illustrative only: '決めなくていいって、言ったよね。'

findings.speaker: kasane
findings.addressee: Tōya (younger brother, in a remembered argument)
findings.text: 必要ない。文面は約束よ。高瀬は開けない。鐘楼も、誰も開けない。
findings.en: It isn't needed. The wording is a promise. Takase won't open it. And no one is opening the bell tower either.
findings.why: Kasane is written they/them (docs/STORY.md; EN 'They were frightened'), and Mio's line in this same scene pulls back from 姉 to 家族 to keep it open. Yet young Kasane's two lines use feminine-coded endings: noun+よ (約束よ) and statement-final の (#5a0b804bcd 書記として言っているの). Kasane uses no such endings anywhere else, so a listener will hear a woman and the deliberate ambiguity is lost.
findings.direction: If the ambiguity is intended, use neutral plain. Illustrative only: '文面は約束だ。' / '書記として言っている。'. If Kasane is meant to read as female, record that in the casting brief instead.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: pc (companion), angry at the unanswered requests
findings.text: 定めには「求め有らば必ず返す」だ。求めは、ここに山ほどある。
findings.en: The charter says "whenever asked, shall return". Here's a mountain of asking.
findings.why: The charter reads 「求め有らば必ず返すべし」 everywhere else (sa.charter_gate, sa.after_battle). Nao's quotation drops べし, which leaves a classical/modern hybrid inside quotation marks. The frame 定めには「…」だ is also not how Japanese introduces a quotation (〜とある, or 定めは「…」だ).
findings.direction: Either quote the charter exactly with a natural frame, or paraphrase it in Nao's own words. Illustrative only: '定めには「求め有らば必ず返すべし」ってある。'

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: Akari and pc (Akari is reading her father's letter, moved)
findings.text: 灯りの下で書かれた手紙は、灯りと同じ重さがあります。
findings.en: A letter written under a lamp weighs the same as the lamp.
findings.why: Nao, Mio and Suzu answer this moment with a human reaction. Ren answers with a maxim whose meaning is opaque (the letter 'weighs the same as the lamp'). It is the oracle-proverb pattern the spec warns against, in a moment that calls for warmth, and Ren already has many such free-standing aphorisms in this part.
findings.direction: Keep Ren's precision but anchor it in what is in front of them. Illustrative only: 'ホシノさんの字ですね。灯りの下で、ゆっくり書いたんでしょう。'

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: 条件、時、結果。三つとも守りました。
findings.en: Condition, timing, consequence. We kept all three.
findings.why: Ren lists the conditional lesson's own categories (〜ないと / 〜たら / 〜なければ as condition, time, result). That is exercise metalanguage, not something said to a companion, and spoken aloud the bare 時 is opaque.
findings.direction: Let Ren react to what happened in his own precise way. Illustrative only: '書いてあるとおりの順番で、閉められました。'

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 貸しじゃないよ。預けるだけ。次の幕まで。……返しに来てよね。必ず。曖昧じゃないほうの必ず。
findings.en: It's not a loan. I'm just leaving it with you. Until the next act. …Come and give it back. Without fail. The kind of "without fail" that isn't vague.
findings.kansai: 貸しちゃうで。預けるだけや。次の幕まで。……返しに来てな。必ず。曖昧ちゃうほうの必ずやで。
findings.why: The Kansai 貸しちゃうで ('it's not a loan': noun 貸し + Kansai ちゃう) sounds exactly like standard casual 貸しちゃう (= 貸してしまう, 'I'll lend it'), which means the opposite. The automated tag already reads it as c:chau. In Suzu's final line, neither listener nor learner should have to stop and parse it.
findings.direction: Use an unambiguous Kansai negative. Illustrative only: '貸しとちゃうで。' or '貸しやないで。'

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 三十年も荷を担いでたの？腰の貸しが、相当溜まってるね。
findings.en: Thirty years of hauling bags? Your back must be owed a fortune.
findings.kansai: 三十年も荷担いではったん？腰の貸しが、相当溜まってるで。
findings.why: The standard line is plain (担いでたの？). The Kansai version adds respectful はる toward the addressee, a light honorific the standard line does not have, then drops straight back to plain (溜まってるで). Elsewhere Suzu's Kansai uses はる only for third persons (サヨさん, タマエさん, ヒロ), never for the person she is talking to.
findings.direction: Keep the politeness parallel. Illustrative only: '三十年も荷担いでたん？'. If Robin wants Kansai Suzu to honour elders with はる, give the standard line the same light respect.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.addressee: pc (companion), in front of the enemy
findings.text: 「はい」で「いいえ」を隠す役者。……化けの皮、はがしてあげましょう。
findings.en: An actor who hides a "no" inside a "yes". …Let's peel off that disguise.
findings.kansai: 「はい」で「いいえ」を隠す役者。……化けの皮、はがしたろ。
findings.why: The standard line uses a theatrical polite volitional with ironic あげる ('let's do it the favour'). The Kansai version becomes plain and rough (〜たろ = 〜てやろう), which changes both the politeness level and the ironic stage tone.
findings.direction: Keep the stagey polite flourish in Kansai. Illustrative only: '化けの皮、はがしたりましょか。'

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: リツの店、帳簿がめちゃくちゃよ。値切られても断れないから、団子が半額以下。
findings.en: Ritsu's accounts are a shambles. She can't refuse when people haggle, so her dango sell for less than half price.
findings.kansai: リツの店、帳簿がめちゃくちゃやで。値切られても断られへんから、団子が半額以下や。
findings.why: 断られへん is a valid Kansai potential ('can't refuse', like 行かれへん), but it is identical to the passive negative ('isn't refused'). Coming right after 値切られても, a learner will read it as passive and miss the point that Ritsu can't say no.
findings.direction: Use 断れへん, which is equally Kansai and unambiguous, or add a note.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 寝坊！……ごめん。でも、これは返してあげてほしいな。十年後には笑い話になるやつだよ。
findings.en: Overslept! …Sorry. But I'd like this one given back. In ten years it'll be a funny story.
findings.kansai: 寝坊！……ごめん。せやけど、これは返したってほしいな。十年後には笑い話になるやつやで。
findings.why: Kansai 返したって (= 返してやって) looks exactly like standard 〜たって 'even if'. The same 〜たる (= 〜てやる) family appears several more times in this part: 知らせたらなあかん (sa.ushio_grave#231a5fc2c2), 幕上げたらなあかん (lf.junction#aac650a54b) where 〜たら is easily mistaken for the conditional, and はがしたろ (lf.boss_intro). None of them is explained.
findings.direction: Add a word-help or register note for Kansai 〜たる / 〜たって / 〜たら (= 〜てやる / 〜てやって / 〜てやら). No text change.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 一番聞かれたくない台詞を、一番先に棚にしまったのか。……分かるよ。分かりたくないけど。
findings.en: The line they least wanted anyone to hear, put on the shelf first of all. …I understand. I wish I didn't.
findings.kansai: 一番聞かれたない台詞を、一番先に棚にしまったんか。……分かるわ。分かりたないけど。
findings.why: Kansai 〜たない (= 〜たくない) appears twice in one line (聞かれたない, 分かりたない). A learner will not recognise 聞かれたくない in 聞かれたない.
findings.direction: Add a word-help note: Kansai 〜たない = 〜たくない. No text change.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: さあさあ、お立ち会い！役所と運河の町、灯落でござい！
findings.en: Roll up, roll up! Behold Lanternfall, city of offices and canals!
findings.why: お立ち会い and 〜でござい are a street barker's call, an old stage register, and right for Suzu. A learner may take でござい for a clipped でございます or think it is ordinary polite speech.
findings.direction: Add a register note saying this is a theatrical barker's call, not for everyday use. No text change.

findings.speaker: sa_tsuzuri
findings.text: ツヅリは、小屋で宿帳を付けています。上りと下り。分類は二つだけ。快適です。
findings.en: Tsuzuri keeps the register at the hut now. Up and down. Only two categories. Very restful.
findings.why: Tsuzuri refers to itself by name (also sa.choose_archive, sa.clerk_name), a deliberate trait of a newly named being. In everyday Japanese, self-reference by name reads as childish, so the learner needs to know it is a character choice, not a model.
findings.direction: Add a short register note: self-reference by name is a deliberate trait of this character. No text change.

findings.speaker: lf_kinu
findings.text: あら、久しぶりに「いいや」を聞きましたわ。
findings.en: My, it's been a while since I heard "no".
findings.why: Polite + わ (〜ましたわ, and 見たいわ in #609aa52a53) is an old-fashioned genteel feminine register. It is right for Kinu, but learners need to know it is a character marker and not a neutral polite ending.
findings.direction: Add a register note on genteel ですわ／ましたわ. No text change.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc (close travelling companion), in front of the council
findings.text: 書庫には、ウシオ師匠の残りもあるはずです。顔も、最後の……口げんかも。
findings.en: The rest of Master Ushio should be in the Archive. His face, and our last… quarrel.
findings.why: This is a literal rendering of 'the rest of Master Ushio'. 「師匠の残り」 sounds like 'Master's leftovers' or 'remains', which is jarring in an emotional line. In Japanese, 残り needs a noun for what is left: memories, the part Ren lost.
findings.direction: Say what remains: the memories of Ushio that Ren lost. Keep Ren's careful polite register and the broken-off 口げんか, e.g. 「ウシオ師匠の、私がなくした記憶も」.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: Umi (recipient Nao wronged; a near-stranger whom Nao calls ウミさん)
findings.text: 一年前に預かった。渡さないと決めた。君に聞かずに。
findings.en: I was given it a year ago. I decided not to deliver it. Without asking you.
findings.why: 「君に聞かずに」 reads like 'without asking you' translated straight from English. Nao calls her ウミさん, and Nao's usual 'you' is あんた, so 君 here sounds bookish and slightly patronising. The same phrasing appears on the :again branch (#8d57b6d8ab), and Nao uses 君 to Umi again in sa.epi_lf, so this may be a deliberate softer pronoun for her. If so, it is the only place Nao uses it, and Robin should confirm it.
findings.direction: Most natural is to drop the pronoun or use her name, e.g. 「……ウミさんに聞きもしないで」 or 「勝手に」. Apply the same change to #8d57b6d8ab.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.addressee: pc and the current companion (old travelling acquaintances; Nao is an NPC here)
findings.text: 鐘、聞こえたよ。あれ、君たちだよね。
findings.en: Heard the bell. That was you lot, right?
findings.why: Everywhere else Nao calls the player あんた, or お前 once they are close. 「君たち」 is softer and more standard than Nao's voice. Spoken, it sounds like another character's line.
findings.direction: Use Nao's usual address or drop the pronoun, e.g. 「あれ、あんたたちだろ」.

findings.speaker: mio
findings.text: それでも、私の口で言いたかったんです。お断りします。
findings.en: Even so, I wanted to say it with my own mouth. I refuse.
findings.why: The idiom is 「自分の口で／自分の口から言いたかった」. 「私の口で」 follows the English 'my own mouth' and sounds slightly off in Mio's most important line. The polite register is right and should stay.
findings.direction: Change only the possessive, e.g. 「自分の口で言いたかったんです」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: Tadashi (the Registrar himself) and the party
findings.text: 元に戻すことを、記録の世界では「復元」と言うそうです。灯守では「灯を入れ直す」と言います。
findings.en: In the world of records they call putting things back "restoration". Lantern keepers call it "relighting".
findings.why: Ren tells the head of the Records Hall what records people call restoration, using a hearsay そうです. It reads as a vocabulary note (復元) that has leaked into dialogue. The lantern-keeper parallel is the part that is in character.
findings.direction: Keep the 灯を入れ直す comparison and drop the lesson to the expert. If 復元 must stay, let Ren ask Tadashi about it or turn it toward him, e.g. 「記録では『復元』ですか。灯守なら『灯を入れ直す』です」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.addressee: pc and Tami, after the minutes are read
findings.text: 「必要なら」。誰にとっての必要かを、誰も書かなかった。灯守の約束も、気をつけないと同じ穴に落ちます。
findings.en: "If it's needed." Nobody wrote down needed by whom. A lantern keeper's promise can fall into the same hole if we aren't careful.
findings.why: 「同じ穴に落ちる」 translates 'fall into the same hole' literally. Japanese says 同じ落とし穴にはまる or 同じ轍を踏む. As written, it sounds slightly off and close to 同じ穴のむじな.
findings.direction: Use the native idiom, e.g. 「同じ落とし穴にはまります」.

findings.speaker: ren
findings.text: 橋の名札が、灯籠の笠と同じ消え方をしています。字だけが、きれいにない。
findings.en: The bridges' plaques have faded the way the lantern shades did. Only the letters gone, and cleanly.
findings.why: 「きれいにない」 is not a natural collocation. きれいに goes with a verb of disappearing: Mio's earlier line in rw.mio_first has 「字だけ、きれいになくなっている」. As written, it reads like a clipped note and is awkward to say aloud.
findings.direction: Add the verb, e.g. 「字だけが、きれいに消えています」.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 貸し借りは、きっちり返してもらいましょう。町一つ分の「いいえ」、利子をつけてね。
findings.en: Let's make sure the debts get settled properly. One whole town's worth of "no"s — with interest.
findings.kansai: 貸し借りは、きっちり返してもらお。町一つ分の「いいえ」、利子つけてな。
findings.why: 「貸し借りは」 means the mutual account, but 「返してもらう」 needs 貸し, what is owed to us. The phrase mixes two set expressions. Suzu is meticulous about debts, so her debt wording should be exact. The KANSAI line has the same mix.
findings.direction: Use 貸し with 返してもらう, or keep 貸し借り with a matching verb, e.g. 「貸しは、きっちり返してもらいましょう」. Apply the same change to KANSAI.

findings.speaker: suzu
findings.text: 行きましょう。……大きな声で呼ぶのは、私の得意よ。
findings.en: Let's go. …Calling out loud is my speciality.
findings.kansai: 行こ。……大きい声で呼ぶのは、うちの得意やで。
findings.why: This is a pattern across the part. Suzu's standard lines often suggest things with 〜ましょう, and the KANSAI versions consistently drop that to plain volitional: 行きましょう→行こ here; also 読んでもらいましょう→読んでもらお (lf.stacks_check#58a5daa137), 返してもらいましょう→返してもらお (lf.yae_after#09dd058a8a, mb.morning_after#526875a6fa), 思い出させてあげましょう→思い出さしてあげよ (mb.firstbridge_arrive#35562a39f3), 始めましょう→始めよか (mb.lc_inside#bd86412067), 幕間にしましょ→幕間にしよう (lf.road_north_locked#5badf1b864). Suzu's ましょう is a playful stage softener rather than deference, so the drop is small. It is still a systematic difference in politeness between the two versions.
findings.direction: Decide one rule. Either the standard lines use plain volitional (行こう) to match Suzu's otherwise plain voice, or KANSAI keeps the soft-suggestion flavour, e.g. 「行きましょ」 or 「行こか」. Note also that 「幕間にしよう」 is standard, not Kansai.

findings.speaker: nao
findings.text: それぞれの荷に、それぞれの行き先か。……守るのも同じだな。一人ずつ、来るものに合わせて。
findings.en: Each load, its own place. …Protecting's the same. One at a time, fitted to what's coming.
findings.why: Take has just talked about routing barges. Every companion branch then jumps to 'protecting' (守る), which no one has mentioned: Nao here, Mio #ff4f491fb2, Ren #2c44bb3dcb, Suzu #56d964e427. The jump exists only to introduce the それぞれを守る skill, so the lesson leaks into the banter. The 待つ beat in mb.sen_dispute does the same job naturally, because mediation is what the scene is about.
findings.direction: Either give the scene a reason to think about protection (a nearby scuffle, a crate about to fall), or keep the companion line on barges and let the narration line 「言葉が一つ、形になった」 make the connection to battle.

findings.speaker: mb_zenzo
findings.text: 壁を崩せる者はおらんかのう。荷運びなら、力があるじゃろうに。
findings.en: Is there no one who can knock that wall through? A porter would have the strength.
findings.why: Zenzō's profile is 'warm, contented warehouse owner', yet he uses the full stock old-man role language (儂, じゃ, のう, おらん, じゃろう, わい in mb.lw_sl_mb_zenzo_r2/r3). Nothing in his character calls for it. The other old men in this part (Tokuji, Tetsu, Heiji, Magobē) and Tsuru elsewhere avoid じゃ. He is also inconsistent: mb.zenzo#fb964494f9 「茶を飲んだよ」 and #c72c605550 「ありがとうよ」 have no marker at all. Kansuke, a sly riddler, can carry the folk-tale voice; Zenzō reads as the default 'old man'.
findings.direction: Robin's call. Either give Zenzō a lighter elder plain (だね／かい、like Tsuru) and keep the role language for Kansuke only, or keep it and make it consistent across his eight lines, with a register note.

findings.speaker: mb_zenzo
findings.text: 塗り込めたのか！……儂の腕じゃ、壁は崩せん。
findings.en: Walled up! …These arms of mine can't break through a wall.
findings.why: A learner needs a note on three things here. 儂 is the elderly-male 'I'. 「腕じゃ」 is the contraction of では, not the copula じゃ that Zenzō uses in the next lines (これじゃ！祖父の字じゃ). 「崩せん」 is the 〜ん negative. Two different じゃ in one speaker's scene is a real trap for learners.
findings.direction: Add a register note: role-language 'old man' speech (儂, copula じゃ = だ, おらん = いない, じゃろう = だろう). Add a word-help note that 腕じゃ = 腕では.

findings.speaker: mb_kansuke
findings.text: 儂のなぞなぞは、もう全部解かれてしもうた。……次に来るまでに、新しいのを考えておこう。
findings.en: You've solved every riddle I have. …By the time you come again, I'll have thought up new ones.
findings.why: 「しもうた」 (= してしまった) is a Western-Japan form used here as old-man role language. Together with おった and のう (#f382f494b0) and じゃ (#bf24f7d651), it is a marked style that a learner will not find in a textbook. Kansuke's playful trickster role justifies it, but the scene gives no note.
findings.direction: Add a register note at Kansuke's first line (#4f71d917ef) or here: folk-tale old-man speech (儂, じゃ, 〜ん, しもうた = してしまった, おった = いた). No text change.

findings.speaker: mb_fujiko
findings.text: 札が読めると、払いも読める。ありがたいね。……次に潮硝子へ行くなら、干物の代金、持っていっておくれ。
findings.en: When the plaques read, so do the payments. A mercy. …If you're going back to Saltglass, take them the money for the fish, would you?
findings.why: 「〜ておくれ」 is an old-fashioned request form, used here by a middle-aged merchant mistress. It fits her brisk 女将 voice, but a learner will not know it as a request form or why it appears.
findings.direction: Add a note: 〜ておくれ = 〜てくれ／〜てちょうだい, an old-fashioned, familiar request used by a senior to a junior. No text change.

findings.speaker: lf_setsu
findings.text: 部屋の数の三倍、お客さまがいらっしゃるんです。ふふ、嬉しいですわ。
findings.en: Three times as many guests as rooms. Heh. It's a pleasure.
findings.why: 「ですわ」 (and ますの in yn.lw_lf_setsu_guest) is a stylised, old-fashioned genteel feminine polite form that is rare in modern speech. It is a deliberate marker for Setsu, as for Kinu, so it should stay. A learner should know it is not a neutral polite ending to copy. Tsuya's 「もちろんですわ」 (lf.tsuya#804a33715a) uses the same form.
findings.direction: Add a register note: ですわ／ますの = refined, old-fashioned feminine polite, a character marker. Ordinary polite speech uses です／ます without わ.

findings.speaker: umi
findings.addressee: Nao (companion; after the letter scene the two speak plainly)
findings.text: 父から、返事の返事が来ました。字がひどく揺れていて、半分しか読めません。……それでいいんです。
findings.en: A reply to my reply came from my father. The writing shakes so badly I can only read half. …That's all right.
